title: Visually Guided Decoding: Gradient-Free Hard Prompt Inversion with Language Models

contributions.purpose: Generate fully interpretable, human-readable hard prompts for text-to-image models without the trial-and-error and incoherence of prior prompt inversion methods.
contributions.mechanism: Visually Guided Decoding (VGD): a gradient-free decoding method that combines an off-the-shelf LLM's token generation (as text prior P(T)) with CLIP-score guidance (approximating P(I|T)) at each decoding step, formulated via a noisy-channel objective argmax P_CLIP(I|T)P_LLM(T)^alpha; no training required.
contributions.evaluation: On Lexica.art and other datasets with Stable Diffusion 2.1, VGD (LLaVA-1.5 backbone) achieves SOTA CLIP-I scores across all four datasets, surpassing the LLaVA-1.5+CLIP-Interrogator baseline; higher BERTScore than PEZ; human preference: 60.5% (image variation) and 52.6% (style transfer) selected VGD.
contributions.source_quote: we propose Visually Guided Decoding (VGD), a gradient-free approach that leverages large language models (LLMs) and CLIP-based guidance to generate coherent and semantically aligned prompts.

contributions.purpose: Show the approach is efficient and model-agnostic, providing a practical drop-in for chat-interfaced image generation.
contributions.mechanism: Being training-free, only the decoding process is modified; compatibility tested across multiple LLMs (LLaMA2, LLaMA3, Mistral) and image models (DALL-E 2, MidJourney, Stable Diffusion 2).
contributions.evaluation: Measured on a single A100 80GB: VGD is 7x faster than Textual Inversion, 12x faster than PEZ, and >2200x faster than PH2P; performance differences across LLMs are marginal (LLaMA3-8B slightly best).
contributions.source_quote: Since VGD seamlessly stitches LLMs and text-to-image models without additional training (i.e., gradient-free), VGD provides a flexible and efficient solution for chat-interfaced image generation services using LLM

self_declared_provenance.quote: Inspired by the noisy channel model (Jurafsky, 2000; Brown et al., 1993), widely used in machine translation and speech recognition, we model the prompt discovery process by integrating an LDM objective with a regularization term for language modeling.

To alleviate this computational burden, we approximate P(I|T) using CLIP, such that P(I|T) approx P_CLIP(I|T). This approximation is justified by the fact that Stable Diffusion utilizes the frozen CLIP text encoder.

notes: Trade-off surfaced in ablation: the 'CLIP only' variant achieves the highest CLIP score but the lowest BERTScore (less coherent/interpretable), while VGD balances both; 'LLM only' collapses on CLIP score. Misaligned CLIP model (ViT-B-32, ViT-L-14) causes significant degradation. Limitation acknowledged: LLaVA baselines beat VGD on BERTScore but lose on CLIP-I. Overall a positive-results paper (ICLR 2025 accept).
